title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor
hook: The concerto that brought Rachmaninoff back after three silent years.

painting.title: Lake. Russia
painting.pairingNote: Levitan’s last large canvas, painted in the same months Rachmaninoff found his way back to composing, a wide and bright Russian summer.

facts: In March 1897 the premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony was a failure, savaged by the critics. He was 23, fell into depression and wrote almost nothing for three years.

From January to April 1900 he saw the physician Nikolai Dahl almost daily for treatment that included hypnosis. He wrote the second and third movements that year, partly in Italy, and finished the first movement in April 1901. The concerto is dedicated to Dahl.

He played the second and third movements in Moscow in December 1900. The complete concerto was first heard on 9 November 1901 in Moscow, with Rachmaninoff at the piano and his cousin Alexander Siloti conducting. It was a success, and it is still his most popular work.

Piano and orchestra are partners here more than rivals. The piano often accompanies while the orchestra has the tune, and the first movement has no [[cadenza|cadenza]]. Its melodies were later borrowed by the film *Brief Encounter* (1945) and by pop songs.
bigPicture.inOneLine: bells and a dark, surging song (I), a still, glowing nocturne (II), a playful chase that ends in a blaze of C major (III).

movements.heading: Moderato
movements.summary: The piano starts alone, like a bell slowly growing louder, and then the orchestra sweeps in with a dark Russian melody. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with two contrasting themes. It has no cadenza: the energy is held back for the moment when the opening theme returns as a march.

mainIdeas.name: The bells
mainIdeas.description: slow piano chords, each answered by a deep note in the bass.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, dark and broad
mainIdeas.description: a long melody in C minor for the strings, with the piano rolling underneath it.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, tender
mainIdeas.description: a wide, lyrical melody in E-flat major, first sung by the piano alone.

stops.hear: The piano alone: slow, heavy chords, each answered by a low note, growing from very soft to very loud
stops.happening: The introduction. Eight bars of tolling chords

stops.hear: Strings and a clarinet play a dark, broad melody; underneath, the piano rolls waves of fast notes
stops.happening: Theme 1, in C minor. The orchestra has the tune; the piano accompanies with [[arpeggio|arpeggio]]s

stops.hear: The melody breaks off; the piano takes the lead in a short, restless passage
stops.happening: The bridge to the second theme

stops.hear: Everything slows and softens; the piano alone sings a tender, wide melody
Piano and orchestra pass the melody back and forth; it rises and swells, then settles
stops.happening: Theme 2 grows. The end of the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: Faster and more anxious; short pieces of Theme 1 chase each other between piano and orchestra

stops.label: Mid-development
stops.hear: A short, stubborn marching figure appears in the piano and keeps coming back, louder each time
stops.happening: The seed of the march to come

stops.hear: The orchestra plays Theme 1 at full strength, slower and grander, while the piano pounds out heavy chords against it
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] and the climax at once: Theme 1 returns as a march, *Maestoso (alla marcia)*

stops.hear: After the storm, a solo horn plays Theme 2 very quietly; the piano answers with a slow, floating line
stops.happening: Theme 2 returns, changed and far away

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Fast and agitated again; the movement ends with short, loud chords in C minor

notice: In the opening chords, listen to the lowest note after each chord. It is the bell’s deep stroke, and it grows with the chords.
When Theme 1 first appears, the piano is busy but does not have the tune. At the march it does not have it either: it pounds out its own rhythm against the orchestra.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Richter recorded the concerto in Warsaw in April 1959, a year and a half before his first concerts in the United States. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by Tchaikovsky’s First Piano Concerto with Karajan.

movements.heading: Adagio sostenuto
movements.summary: A slow movement in a warm E major, after the C minor of the first. A simple, songlike melody passes from flute to clarinet to piano, over a gently rocking accompaniment. In the middle the music becomes more animated, rises to a climax and a short piano cadenza, and then the melody comes back.

mainIdeas.name: The rocking figure
mainIdeas.description: broken chords in the piano that never stop moving.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a long, slow, simple melody, first on the flute.

stops.hear: Soft, [[muted|muted]] string chords that slowly shift; the dark colour melts into a warmer one
stops.happening: A short introduction that moves from C minor to E major

stops.hear: The piano enters alone with a gentle, rocking pattern of broken chords
stops.happening: The accompaniment that runs through most of the movement

stops.hear: Above the piano, a solo flute plays a long, slow, simple melody
A solo clarinet takes over the melody and carries it further
stops.happening: The theme continues in a darker, warmer colour

stops.hear: The piano now sings the melody itself; the strings answer
The music moves faster; quick, dancing figures in the piano, answered in turn by bassoon, horn and violas
A rush of fast notes builds to a loud climax; then the piano alone plays a brief, brilliant flourish
The violins sing the main theme; the piano returns to its rocking pattern

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The piano alone plays soft, rising chords; the movement ends quietly in E major

notice: Follow the piano’s rocking figure. It hardly stops for the whole movement, even when the melody moves elsewhere.
Compare the flute and the clarinet in the opening minutes. It is the same melody; only the colour changes.

movements.heading: Allegro scherzando
movements.summary: After a quiet build-up the piano crashes in with a quick, jumpy theme. Its opposite is one of Rachmaninoff’s most famous melodies, broad and longing. The two alternate, and at the end the longing melody returns in the full orchestra, now in C major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, playful
mainIdeas.description: a fast, jumpy tune in C minor, mostly for the piano. *Scherzando* means “playfully”.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, the big tune
mainIdeas.description: a long, warm, sad melody, first on oboe and violas together.

stops.hear: A quiet, quick march in the orchestra that keeps building
stops.happening: The introduction, moving from E major back towards C minor

stops.hear: The piano bursts in with a sweeping flourish
A fast, jumpy, nervous tune in the piano, with crisp chords in the orchestra
The music relaxes; oboe and violas play a long, warm, longing melody
stops.happening: Theme 2, in B-flat major. It later became the song “Full Moon and Empty Arms” (1945)

stops.hear: The piano takes up the melody in rich chords
Theme 1 returns and is tossed between piano and orchestra; at one point the instruments enter one after another with the same quick tune
The warm melody returns, now in a different key, on oboe and strings and then the piano
Rising scales and a long build; the tension climbs
The whole orchestra plays the warm melody at full strength, now in C major; the piano crashes out chords
stops.happening: Theme 2 as the climax (*Maestoso*), played [[tutti|tutti]]. The minor has become major

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: A fast dash to the end, and a burst of loud closing chords

notice: Theme 2 appears three times: on oboe and violas, then in a new key, then in C major for everyone. Notice how it becomes broader each time.
The concerto began in C minor with lonely piano chords. It ends in C major with piano and orchestra together.

threads.title: Darkness to light
threads.body: The concerto moves from C minor to C major. The last movement’s big tune is the moment the minor finally turns major.

threads.title: Bells
threads.body: The opening chords sound like Russian church bells. Rachmaninoff later wrote a whole choral symphony called *The Bells* (1913).

threads.title: Partners, not rivals
threads.body: The piano often accompanies the orchestra instead of competing with it, and the big moments arrive when the two join forces.

threads.title: Long melodies
threads.body: Each movement has a melody that keeps unfolding without seeming to stop for breath.
